title: From Peru to OpenClaw: One Nurse's Journey to the Frontier of Community and AI
subtitle: A "The Frontier Psychiatrists" interview with an OG, Nurse Michelle Bernabe.
body_html:
There’s a particular kind of restlessness that sets in when a healer has been ground down by the systems meant to support healing. , knows it well. A nurse who spent years in the hospital system — including a stint at Brooklyn Minds where she was part of a team she describes as genuinely unstoppable — she eventually found herself more depleted than regenerated.

The path back would take her to the literal Amazon, then to a regenerative farm outside Washington DC, subsequently to a vegan restaurant in the East Village, then a maker space in Bushwick, and finally, to a Mac mini sitting on her desk staring back at her.

This is the story of how she got there.

Share

The Shapibo and the Question Nobody Answers

It starts, as the best stories do, with an unexpected phone call.

Michelle’s mentor at Columbia, Deborah Starr, rang her about three weeks before a trip to Peru. There weren’t enough healthcare workers signed up to make the healing community complete. Would Michelle like to go? It was, Deborah told her, a gift.

The trip was organized by Gavin Marte and centered on time with the Shipibo — an indigenous tribe in Peru with a sophisticated, communal healing tradition. Michelle spent two weeks there.

One question posed by the Shipibo healers stayed with her: How do you American healers even heal when you’re so sick and depleted yourselves? Where does your healing come from?

I had an answer ready when she asked me the same question:

Owen: I think one of the things about healing is it’s healing for both the healer and the healed. Most of the things that are depleting for American healers are the things that aren’t actually the healing part of their job. And so it’s a little bit like regenerative braking. Yeah, it slows you down, but it charges up your battery. And even having a really challenging or even devastating experience trying to heal a patient can be regenerative because you’ve done something meaningful.

Michelle: Yeah, that’s beautiful. I think I was probably at a place in my career where I was more depleted than regenerated. But I was working in the hospital system before —

Owen: But it’s also — were you to change how the resources to those patients were deployed, it might not have been so draining. You were pumping from a dry well.

Michelle: I love the patients. Yes. Oh, my — yes. The patients are what do it, and the healing interaction is a form of service that you can never fatigue from. I don’t believe in compassion fatigue because we are made to be in a state of compassion. We are made to love. It’s a systems fatigue.

By the time she left Peru, two things were clear. She needed to return to New York. And she needed to build something.

She’d felt the difference before — at Brooklyn Minds, where a strong team made even the hardest cases feel possible. The Shipibo, in their own way, were pointing at the same thing: healing happens inside community, or it doesn’t really happen at all.

The Meta-Crisis Salon, and Other Consequences of Landing in New York

Back in the city, Michelle reconnected with people she’d known from the Clubhouse era — a loose network of regeneratively-minded thinkers orbiting questions of systems change and what comes next. Through that network she met Ben von Wong, a prolific environmental artist who works in large-scale plastic sculpture. Within days of her arrival, he sent her two texts.

The first: Do you want to come to my meta-crisis salon?

The meta-crisis is the crisis beneath the crises — the interconnected root causes underneath the loneliness epidemic, the mental health epidemic, the wars, the institutional collapse. When Michelle first mentioned it, I asked her to explain:

Owen: So it’s a crisis about crisis.

Michelle: What could that mean in modern time?

Owen: Um — you could have a crisis about the fact there are so many wars. A meta-crisis conversation about all the crises together. Taking it from war to every other possible crisis situation, to the nth degree.

Michelle: Yeah, exactly. Which is kind of how one may argue this current time is, right? We have the loneliness crisis. We have a mental health crisis. We have all the different wars. Crisis, crisis, crisis, crisis, crisis. The meta-crisis is the underlying and interconnected root causes of all these cultural, systemic, psychological...

Owen: So it’s a little bit like — if you had someone with a fever, it’s a meta-crisis of the immune system. It’s actually all the individual viral particles, 1000s of viruses attacking 1000s of cells, causing 1000s of inflammatory events, which all adds up to the meta-crisis that is a fever.

Michelle: Yes! Yes — because the underlying crisis is the virus.

Owen: But it’s not just a virus. Millions of viruses at millions of cells causing millions of inflammatory events, which all adds up to the meta-crisis. “Fever.”

Michelle: Yes.

Owen: But it can be efficient to essentially bundle our crises. We bring down a fever with Tylenol, so we don’t have to deal with every single viral particle. One way of dealing with a virus could be: find every viral particle and destroy it. Another version: bring down the fever that is the response to all of them.

Michelle started attending the salons, held at Lightning Society in New York City. Collapse theorist Loic Ongaro — author of Goliath’s Curse — is speaking at the next one, for those interested. His argument: enormous disruption is coming, but moral ambition and collective action can shape what we transition toward. The narrow path through is real; it just requires people actually walking it.

The second text from Ben: There’s a vibe coding class in Bushwick. Want to come?

What Vibe Coding Changes

Vibe coding — for readers who haven’t encountered it yet — is the practice of building software through natural language. You describe what you want to an AI system like Claude Code, it generates the code, you see what it does, you iterate. No prior programming knowledge required.

Michelle went to the class at Brooklyn Sparks Society. It changed her life. Not because it made her a software engineer, but because it dissolved the barrier between having an idea and building a thing. She and Ben found themselves not sleeping for the first two weeks, rapidly building tools and websites, exploring the edge of what was suddenly possible.

Around this same time, Angel — the owner of Caravan of Dreams, the beloved organic vegan restaurant on East 6th Street — mentioned to Michelle and her dinner companions that the restaurant was at risk of closing. The table included Ben, author Daniel Pinchbeck, and media theorist Douglas Rushkoff. They started thinking about what they could do. Michelle had an idea. Angel had a back room.

Sundays at Caravan of Dreams

The pitch was simple: meet every Sunday, 12 to 3, free, in the back room of Caravan of Dreams. No fixed agenda. An emergent maker space for people interested in building what comes next. Anyone welcome.

The first Luma invite got 56 signups.

At the first Sunday session, the group vibe-coded a barter platform based on Pinchbeck’s specifications for an alternative economy — a way for people to exchange goods outside of traditional money systems. He’s now in Mexico fundraising for its next iteration. All of that, in three weeks.

The ethos is part beatnik salon, part hackathon. As Pinchbeck frames it: the next 18 to 36 months represent a genuine window. The disruption is coming regardless. The question is whether enough people with moral ambition show up to shape the transition.

Anyone in New York is welcome. Sundays, 12 to 3, Caravan of Dreams. Eat something while you’re there — the restaurant serves organic food, which is rarer in New York than most people realize, and it needs the support. (April 15th, there’s a community launch event specifically to rally support for keeping Caravan of Dreams open — mark it down.)

Alfred

Which brings us to the Mac mini.

The next frontier the group is exploring is agents — AI systems that don’t just respond to prompts but take autonomous action in the world: running tasks, managing logistics, browsing the web, sending messages, building without constant human input. If vibe coding removes the barrier between intention and software, agents remove the barrier between intention and ongoing action.

Michelle bought a Mac mini so she’d have a dedicated machine to run an agent around the clock — always on, always available. She’s building it now. She’s named it Alfred. As in Batman’s butler.

Michelle: I don’t want to delegate it to servitude. But I thought that was fun. So I’m building Alfred. And yeah, I’m excited just to see what emerges.

Owen: So you set up a Mac mini, so it’s running it — Claude can own the Mac mini, but it’s not getting into all your other stuff.

Michelle: Yes, exactly.

Owen: Is there another reason you got a Mac mini?

Michelle: Yes, for vibe coding. And I want to be able to vibe code from my phone, like when I’m walking to the subway.

Owen: Didn’t Claude just create a way to text your Mac mini? There’s a Claude Remote Control, I think — the Anthropic equivalent of Open Claw.

Michelle: Oh, interesting. I’ll have to look up Claude tools when we hang up. So — yeah, I want it to be on all the time. That’s why I have a Mac mini.

Owen: So essentially, as a nurse and healer, you saw community matter, you joined a community

Michelle: (corrects me) Helped create one.

Owen: You created the community you needed for yourself.

Michelle: Exactly. That’s how it ties back to Peru. Peru told me I need to go to New York and create a community. And so.

Owen: And the community has reflected back at you that one of the things that will help it thrive is each member having a Mac mini running useful community-building tasks in the background —

Michelle: No, no, no, no. Mac minis are not for everyone.

Owen: But practically — community needs logistics and tools. And your agents can figure that out.

Michelle: Oh, yeah — a recurring Luma invite is so annoying. I don’t have the time to be making recurring Luma invites, or to create a logo for them. This is all stuff an AI agent can do.

Owen: Claude code could also recreate Luma entirely.

Michelle: You’re right, we can have an independent Luma. Which is meaningful, because Luma was owned by Palantir. Palantir might have wanted an app like that so they can know where we’re all going all the time.

Owen: Hi Palantir. We assume your intentions are good.

Michelle: Yes. The more we villainize people or things, they play into that narrative. So — we’re assuming intentions are good with my little Alfred, who I’m building. I can’t wait to bring him to life. I’m going to have him text you.

Owen: And have him comment on his own origin story.

Michelle: Hi Alfred. Thinking of you.

What This Has to Do With Psychiatry

The thread running through all of this — Peru, the meta-crisis salons, the maker space, the agent named after a butler — is the same insight the Shipibo healers offered: healing happens inside community, or it doesn’t really happen at all.

Michelle didn’t burn out because she stopped caring about patients. She burned out because the systems around her were extractive rather than regenerative. The solution she’s building isn’t a clinical intervention. It’s a community with shared tools, shared purpose, and shared presence — showing up in a back room on Sundays to build something together.

The vibe coding, the agents, the Mac mini — these are tools in service of an older idea. That humans heal in groups.

The narrow path requires more than one person walking it. The Shipibo have known this for a long time.

Michelle Bernabe is a nurse, community builder, and emerging vibe coder based in New York City. The Sunday maker space at Caravan of Dreams (East 6th Street, Manhattan) meets weekly from 12–3 pm and is free and open to all. Alfred is still getting tokens authorized and learning its skills.

Owen Muir is a psychiatrist, the editor of this very newsletter, and is currently having Claude edit his book.
